m. acc. sg.; compound (see Samāsa); qualifies आश्रमम्

sandhi.rule: एतत्तदोः सुलोपोऽकोरनञ्समासे हलि (6.1.132); अकः सवर्णे दीर्घः (6.1.101)
sandhi.note: सः drops its visarga before t; तत्र + आश्रमम्: a + ā → ā.
Final t becomes d before the voiced d; printed with virāma and a space.
a + ā → ā. The final m becomes anusvāra before the m of मुनि- (मोऽनुस्वारः, 8.3.23).

samasa.literal: of the choicest among the twice-born
samasa.alt: Equally read as ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa द्विजानां वर्यः; the sense is the same.

samasa.literal: strewn with calmed beasts of prey
samasa.sense: a hermitage where even predators had become peaceful

samasa.vigraha: मुनेः शिष्याः मुनिशिष्याः (ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa); मुनिशिष्यैः उपशोभितम्
samasa.type: tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa containing a ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa
samasa.sense: made beautiful by the presence of Medhas’s disciples
samasa.alt: मुनिशिष्य can also be a dvandva, मुनयश्च शिष्याश्च ‘sages and disciples’; the singular sage of the verse (द्विजवर्यस्य मेधसः) favours ‘the sage’s disciples’.

morph.note: s-aorist of √दृश्: augment अ-, vṛddhi and metathesis of the root (दृश् → द्राक्), the aorist s (here ष after k), and the ending -ईत्. The present stem is the suppletive पश्य-; the aorist uses the root itself.
Genitive singular of the s-stem मेधस्; the same form could be nominative/accusative plural of a different stem, but the sense here is ‘of Medhas’. The name means ‘intelligence, wisdom’.

mantras.anvaya: सः तत्र द्विजवर्यस्य मेधसः प्रशान्तश्वापदाकीर्णं मुनिशिष्योपशोभितम् आश्रमम् अद्राक्षीत्।
mantras.anvaya_en: Subject, place, the owner of the hermitage (genitive), two compound adjectives of the object, the object, and the verb.
mantras.lit: There he saw the hermitage of Medhas, best of the twice-born, filled with beasts of prey grown peaceful and graced by the sage’s disciples.
mantras.tr: There he came upon the hermitage of Medhas, foremost of brahmins — a place where even the wild beasts had grown gentle, graced by the sage’s disciples.

comm.t: The turning point of the frame story. In the forest the king finds Medhas, who will become his teacher; the rest of the Devī Māhātmya is Medhas’s answer to his question (1.40 onward).
Predators living peacefully around a sage is a common sign, in epic and Purāṇic description, of the power of an ascetic’s calm. The setting shows what Suratha does not yet have.

sandhi.type: visarga sandhi (सः); no change of t
sandhi.note: सः loses its visarga before k. The t of कंचित् stays unvoiced before the unvoiced s; the words are only written together.
Visarga before c becomes s, then palatal ś next to c; च + इतः → चेतः (a + i → e).
Final n before t becomes ṃs: विचरन् → विचरंस्.

samasa.vigraha: मुनिषु वरः मुनिवरः (saptamī tatpuruṣa); मुनिवरस्य आश्रमः, तस्मिन्
samasa.type: ṣaṣṭhī tatpuruṣa containing a saptamī tatpuruṣa
samasa.literal: in the hermitage of the best among sages

morph.note: Perfect of √स्था: reduplication त- (the s of the cluster is dropped, the stop kept and deaspirated) and the ending -औ of ā-roots in the first and third singular.
Accusative of the interrogative किम् with the indefinite particle -चित्: कम् + चित् ‘some (one)’. With कालम् it is an accusative of duration: ‘for some time’.
Present participle of वि + √चर्, nominative singular masculine (stem विचरत्): ‘while wandering’, simultaneous with तस्थौ.

mantras.anvaya: तेन मुनिना सत्कृतः सः तस्मिन् मुनिवराश्रमे इतः च इतः च विचरन् कंचित् कालं तस्थौ च।
mantras.anvaya_en: Main verb तस्थौ with an accusative of time; the participles सत्कृतः and विचरन् describe the subject. च joins this to the previous verse’s action.
mantras.lit: And he stayed for some time, honoured by that sage, wandering here and there in that hermitage of the excellent sage.
mantras.tr: Welcomed with honour by the sage, he stayed there for a while, wandering here and there about the great sage’s hermitage.

comm.t: Suratha is received as a guest and stays. He has not yet asked anything; his wandering ‘here and there’ prepares the restless thoughts of the next verses.
A modern reading: the body is at rest in a peaceful place, the mind is not. Outer refuge does not by itself settle inner turmoil.

sandhi.note: Before a vowel the special rule for सः (6.1.132) does not apply; सः behaves like any -aḥ: so + a → so’ with avagraha.
The compound stem मद् (‘I, my’) ends in t before the unvoiced p.
Final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra, four times in one line.

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (its first part ममत्वाकृष्ट is a tṛtīyā tatpuruṣa: ममत्वेन आकृष्टा)
samasa.literal: one whose mind is pulled by mine-ness
samasa.sense: possessed by the thought ‘this is mine’
samasa.alt: चेतन (n.) ‘mind’ may be the last member instead of चेतना (f.); the bahuvrīhi ends in -चेतनः either way.

samasa.sense: by my ancestors, the earlier kings of my line

morph.note: ममत्व is the genitive मम ‘of me’ made into an abstract noun with -त्व: ‘mine-ness’, possessiveness. The word returns in 1.41 and 1.44 (ममत्वाकृष्टमानसौ), where the king and the merchant both confess it.
Participle of √हा ‘to leave’ (हीन ‘left, lacking’). With an instrumental it means ‘deprived of’: मया हीनम् ‘deprived of me’.

mantras.anvaya: तदा तत्र ममत्वाकृष्टचेतनः सः अचिन्तयत् — पूर्वं मत्पूर्वैः पालितं मया हीनं तत् पुरं हि …
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line introduces the king’s thought; the second line begins it (the thought runs to 1.16), with पुरम् the subject of पाल्यते in 1.13.
mantras.lit: Then, there, he, his mind drawn by possessiveness, thought: ‘That city, protected formerly by my forefathers, now deprived of me —
mantras.tr: Then, his mind still held by the sense of ‘mine’, he brooded: ‘That city my forefathers once protected, now bereft of me —
mantras.tr_note: ‘Now’ is supplied for the contrast with पूर्वम्; the sentence is completed in 1.13.

comm.t: The cause of Suratha’s grief is named at once: ममत्व, the feeling of ‘mine’. His thoughts (1.12–16) are a list of things he no longer owns — city, elephant, servants, treasury.

ममत्व is the theme of the frame story. At the end the merchant asks the Goddess for the knowledge that removes ‘mine’ and ‘I’ (13.18: ममेत्यहमिति … सङ्गविच्युतिकारकम्), while the king asks for his kingdom (13.17).

Lalitā Sahasranāma (Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa) names the Goddess as free of and destroying this very thing: names 164 निर्ममा and 165 ममताहन्त्री. The two texts are distinct; the shared idea is the possessiveness the Goddess removes.

sandhi.note: Visarga before t becomes s (भृत्यैस्तैः); after ai it stands as r before a vowel (तैरसद्) and before the voiced dh (वृत्तैर्धर्मतः).
The stem मद् keeps its voiced d before bh; the same in असद्वृत्तैः (असत् + वृत्त).
सः loses its visarga before p; प्रधानः before the voiced m becomes प्रधानो.

samasa.sense: by the officers he left behind — the ministers of 1.8

samasa.type: bahuvrīhi (असत् is a nañ tatpuruṣa: न सत्)
samasa.literal: by those whose conduct is not good

samasa.sense: an elephant always in musth — the sign of a prized war-elephant

morph.note: Passive present of the curādi root √पाल्: the causative-type -अय- is dropped before the passive -य-, giving पाल्य-ते. The subject is पुरम् from 1.12.
Present ātmanepada first singular of √ज्ञा (stem जानी-/जाना-, here जान- + -ए). न जाने ‘I do not know’ introduces the next worry, which runs into 1.14.

mantras.anvaya: (तत् पुरं) तैः असद्वृत्तैः मद्भृत्यैः धर्मतः पाल्यते न वा (इति) न जाने। सः मे प्रधानः सदामदः शूरहस्ती …
mantras.anvaya_en: न जाने governs the question पाल्यते न वा; the second line begins a new subject (the elephant), whose verbs are in 1.14.
mantras.lit: ‘— whether it is protected according to dharma by those servants of mine of bad conduct, or not, I do not know. That chief war-elephant of mine, always in rut —
mantras.tr: is it being ruled justly by those faithless servants of mine, or not? I cannot know. And my chief war-elephant, ever in rut —
mantras.tr_note: न जाने is attached to the first question in the literal version; the readable one lets it stand between the two worries, as the line does.

comm.t: Two worries: whether his city is ruled rightly, and what has become of his favourite elephant. The king still thinks as an owner — ‘my servants’, ‘my elephant’ (मे).
A modern reading: the grief is real but oddly specific. Loss often attaches itself to one cherished thing — here an elephant — that stands for the whole of what was taken.

sandhi.note: Final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra.
Before the unvoiced k the visarga stays a visarga. The final n of कान् is then unchanged before the bh of भोगान्.
मम + अनुगताः: a + a → ā. Then -āḥ before the voiced n: the visarga becomes y, and y is lost before a consonant, leaving अनुगता.

samasa.alt: मम qualifies only the first member (‘my enemies’ control’). Strictly a word outside a compound should not qualify a member inside it, but such constructions are common in epic and Purāṇic verse. मम could also go with यातः loosely (‘gone from me’), but ‘my enemies’ is the natural reading.

samasa.vigraha: प्रसादः च धनं च भोजनं च, तैः
samasa.sense: by the patronage, gifts and meals the king gave them

morph.note: Simple future of उप + √लभ् (ātmanepada root): लभ् + स्य → लप्स्य- (bh → p before s), with the ending -ते. ‘Will it obtain?’
With a verb of motion the kta is active: ‘having gone (into the enemies’ power)’. The subject is the elephant of 1.13.
Active kta of अनु + √गम्, nominative plural: ‘(those who) followed (me)’. The relative clause ये … अनुगताः is answered by ते in 1.15.

mantras.anvaya: (सः शूरहस्ती) मम वैरिवशं यातः कान् भोगान् उपलप्स्यते? ये प्रसादधनभोजनैः नित्यं मम अनुगताः, (ते …)
mantras.anvaya_en: The first line completes the elephant sentence of 1.13; the second opens a relative clause whose main clause (ते … कुर्वन्ति) is in 1.15.
mantras.lit: ‘— having gone into the power of my enemies, what enjoyments will it obtain? Those who always followed me, through favours, wealth and meals —
mantras.tr: now fallen into my enemies’ hands, what comforts will it find? And those who always followed me, won by my favour, my gifts and my table —

comm.t: The king pities his elephant, then turns to his retainers, who were bound to him by what he gave: favour, money and food. The next verse says where their loyalty has gone.
A modern reading: loyalty bought with favour, wealth and food follows the giver of those things, not the person. Suratha half sees this, and still grieves.
